[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental studies using variation in high-skilled immigration (e.g., H-1B visa lotteries or regional visa allocation rules) linked to local labor market and housing data in low-R&D OECD regions, with housing supply elasticity measured via the Saiz (2010) index. — Such designs can isolate the causal effect of high-skilled immigration on non-tradable service sector wages, testing whether the negative wage effect is mediated by housing cost increases and amplified in inelastic housing markets.

[PATH:empirical] Cross-region panel data analysis combining local housing supply elasticity, R&D intensity (e.g., patent counts or R&D employment share), and high-skilled immigrant inflows from administrative or census sources over a 1–3 year lag. — This would directly test the interaction effect of low R&D intensity and inelastic housing supply on the wage-depression channel, controlling for local demand shocks and worker mobility.

[PATH:theoretical] Monocentric city model extensions incorporating heterogeneous worker skill types and a non-tradable sector with housing as a consumption good, calibrated to low-R&D region characteristics. — A formal model can clarify the mechanisms—whether housing cost increases reduce local demand for non-tradable services, thereby lowering wages for native workers, and under what conditions the effect is amplified by supply inelasticity.
